headline: Wrong AI suggestions cut proxy-clinician accuracy from 70% to 50% (20-point drop); offline Q = +0.30 and double-fault rate 3%, with both gates passing on 36 MedQA cases.
idea: A second reader only reduces error insofar as it fails on **different cases** from the first. Two readers that are both 90% accurate can have wildly different double-fault rates depending on whether their errors overlap — the deciding property is error *complementarity*, not accuracy.

The paired-error audit operationalises this: record a 2x2 of case-level outcomes (shared success, model-only error, clinician-only error, shared error), compute the double-fault rate and Yule's Q, stratify by case type, and apply two pre-specified go/no-go gates before deployment.

Independence is fragile: a reader that sees the other's answer first systematically shifts toward it, converting rescue potential into correlated failure. Governance must therefore preserve the measured independence — the offline audit only tells you what *could* be rescued, not what will be in practice.
findings: **Offline 2x2 (N = 36):** The Haiku proxy-clinician reached 78% accuracy and the Sonnet model under audit 92%. Their errors overlapped in just 1 case (shared error), giving a double-fault rate of 2.8% vs 1.9% that independent errors would predict. Yule's Q = +0.30 (bootstrap 95% CI –0.52 to +0.91) — modest positive association but with a very wide interval at this sample size. Rescue potential was high: 7 of 8 cases where the clinician was wrong but the model was right (87.5%).

**Assisted workflows:** When the model answered second after seeing the clinician's impression, it copied a wrong impression 17.6% of the time vs 5.9% when blind — 2 answers switched, both right-to-wrong, trimming rescue from 94% to 82%. The clinician-defers workflow was starker: faced with wrong AI suggestions, the proxy clinician's accuracy on those cases dropped from 70% to 50%, a **20-percentage-point** fall. The paper cites 14–18 pp drops for real physicians (Qazi et al., 2026); this run, with a small LLM proxy, lands at 20 pp — directionally consistent but not directly comparable.

**Gates:** Gate 1 (model accuracy ≥ 80% and double-fault ≤ 5%) passed; Gate 2 (model-only error ≤ 10% and rescue retained ≥ 50%) also passed, driven by the model-only rate of 5.6% and rescue-retained ratio of 87.5%. By stratum, **diagnosis** and **mechanism/other** both cleared Gate 1, but **management** failed (double-fault 8.3%, n = 12) — the paper's partial-deployment logic would flag that stratum for closer review.

**Simulator panel:** Three hypothetical models all at 90% accuracy next to a 78%-accurate clinician span from 0.0% double-fault (complementary) to 10.0% (redundant). The complementary model rescues every clinician error; the redundant model rescues only 54.5%. This run's observed double-fault (2.8%) sits between independent (2.2%) and complementary, as the wide CI illustrates: 36 cases are not enough to tell them apart.

try_next.label: Same-family readers (both Haiku)
try_next.why: Replacing the large audit model with a second Haiku should push Q higher and double-fault up — the same family of errors — testing whether model-model diversity is lower than proxy-clinician/model diversity (Zoller et al., 2025).

try_next.label: Pure conformity test (always-wrong anchors)
try_next.why: Setting anchor_source to always_wrong removes any ambiguity: every anchor shown is guaranteed wrong. This isolates maximum-signal conformity — how often does each reader copy a known-wrong answer when they would otherwise be correct?

try_next.label: Focus on management questions only
try_next.why: Management was the only stratum that failed Gate 1 in this run (double-fault 8.3%). Running on management alone with more cases would give a narrower CI and show whether that stratum is consistently problematic or a small-sample artefact.

caveats: Both readers are LLMs (Claude Haiku as clinician proxy, Claude Sonnet as model under audit). This is an **LLM-vs-LLM proxy** of the clinician–model audit; it does not constitute evidence about how clinicians actually reason or defer, and the automation-bias drop (20 pp) should not be compared directly to physician studies.

MedQA-USMLE multiple-choice exam questions are not real clinical cases — they are constructed items with known key errors and a narrow answer format. Performance here does not predict performance on free-text clinical decisions.

N = 36 is far below the paper's ~1,000-case sizing recommendation for rare serious-harm events. Every rate on this card carries a very wide 95% CI (the double-fault CI spans 0%–14%), and the per-stratum analyses (n ≈ 12 each) are illustrative only.

Gate thresholds (accuracy ≥ 80%, double-fault ≤ 5%, model-only ≤ 10%, rescue retained ≥ 50%) are the runbook defaults, not validated or endorsed by the paper's authors. LLM answers can vary between runs even at temperature 0.
